appraisal_events.evidence: On hearing that Amanien is just dead, the duke says only "Il est mort ! Mais non, on exagère, on exagère !" and immediately returns to fussing over his costume helmet and shoes; the narrator explicitly reads the garbled phrase as expressing "la détermination de ne pas renoncer à un plaisir."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator directly interprets the duke's brushing off of a friend's death as motivated by his refusal to let it spoil the costume ball, locally diminishing him as frivolous and self-absorbed.

appraisal_events.evidence: Françoise hastily hides her daughter's abundant supper, claims she "vient de prendre une cuillère de soupe," and sends her to bed insisting she has "assez travaillé," because Françoise "voulait que sa fille eût l'air... de se tuer au travail pour nous."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes Françoise's staged performance of frugality and self-sacrifice in front of him, locally undercutting her sincerity even as the tone remains affectionate.

status_effects.explanation: The duke is clearly diminished by the narrator's framing of his callous, grammatically garbled dismissal of the death news in favor of preserving his evening's pleasure.
Françoise is somewhat diminished as the narrator reveals the theatrical, self-serving quality of her display of maternal severity and household frugality.

ambiguities: The narrator's tone toward Françoise mixes affection with irony (he calls her language 'beau français populaire'), so the diminishment is milder and less censorious than the treatment of the duke.
